lessons.title: Case Study: Semiconductors, the Taiwan Chokepoint and the Global Fab Race

children.text: Nearly every advanced chip inside the smartphone in your pocket, the GPU training an AI model, and the control unit in a modern car was fabricated within a roughly 100-kilometre radius of Hsinchu, Taiwan. That single fact, more than any tariff schedule or subsidy programme covered so far in this course, explains why semiconductors sit at the centre of nearly every conversation about supply chain risk today. This lesson is a case study in concentration risk at its most extreme: one company, in one geography, sitting between the world's economy and one of the most contested pieces of geography on the planet.

body.text: Semiconductor supply chains are not just concentrated by country, they are concentrated by company. Understanding TSMC's specific role, not just "Taiwan's" role, is the difference between a vague geopolitical worry and an analyzable risk.

children.text: Why TSMC, Specifically, Matters This Much

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, founded in 1987, pioneered a business model that reshaped the entire chip industry: the pure-play foundry, a company that manufactures chips designed by others but designs none of its own. That single innovation let companies like Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm become fabless, focusing entirely on chip design while outsourcing the extraordinarily expensive business of building and running fabrication plants. Today, TSMC commands roughly 60% of the entire global pure-play foundry market by revenue, and for the most advanced process nodes, the cutting-edge chips inside flagship phones and AI accelerators, its share of global production runs well above 90%, since only Samsung competes at that frontier at all, and with meaningfully lower yields.

body.context: For the most advanced process nodes; roughly 60% of the entire global pure-play foundry market across all nodes combined.

markDefs.definition: The theory, named in a 2001 book by journalist Craig Addison, that Taiwan's dominance of advanced chip manufacturing deters a Chinese attack, since the resulting global economic damage would be catastrophic enough to guarantee major-power intervention on Taiwan's behalf.

children.text: This concentration has produced a genuine strategic debate known as the

theory: the idea that Taiwan's chip dominance itself deters conflict, because the global economic damage from disrupting it would be so severe that other major powers have an overwhelming incentive to prevent or respond to any attack. The counter-argument is just as important for an investor to understand: every fab the CHIPS Act, the EU Chips Act and TSMC's own overseas expansion build outside Taiwan very slightly weakens that shield, since it makes the rest of the world marginally less dependent, and therefore, this argument goes, marginally less compelled to intervene.

columns.label: Argument for the shield holding
points: Even diversified fabs abroad still rely on Taiwan for the most advanced nodes
Rebuilding leading-edge capacity elsewhere will take a decade or more
Global economic interdependence on Taiwan remains extremely high in the near term

columns.label: Argument the shield is weakening
points: Every new overseas fab reduces marginal dependence on Taiwan specifically
Governments are explicitly funding diversification for this exact strategic reason
A shield that motivates its own erosion is, by definition, temporary

children.text: The Global Fab Race: Diversifying Away From Taiwan

Chapter 2 already covered the subsidy programmes funding this diversification. TSMC's own response has been to build overseas fabs directly, in Arizona under the CHIPS Act framework, in Kumamoto, Japan through a joint venture with Sony and Denso that began mass production in 2024, and in Dresden, Germany through a joint venture with Bosch, Infineon and NXP focused on automotive and industrial chips. The critical detail every investor needs to hold onto is what kind of chips move where: TSMC has stated consistently that its most advanced process nodes will remain concentrated in Taiwan for the foreseeable future, with overseas fabs handling mature and slightly-behind-the-frontier nodes. Geographic diversification, so far, is happening mostly at the trailing edge, not the leading edge.

children.text: What a Severe Disruption Would Mean, and What It Would Not

Think tanks have modelled the economic cost of a severe disruption to Taiwan's chip production, with some estimates putting global economic activity at risk in the low trillions of dollars annually, though these figures vary enormously by methodology and should be read as illustrative scenario modelling, not forecasts. What matters more for how you actually use this case study is the structural takeaway: India has essentially no direct exposure to Taiwan's most advanced chip nodes today, since its own semiconductor ambitions, covered in depth in Chapter 4, focus on assembly, testing and mature-node fabrication rather than the cutting edge. India's exposure would instead be indirect and severe: any global disruption to advanced chips would ripple immediately into every consumer electronics, automotive and IT hardware supply chain feeding into Indian assembly plants and export orders.

body.text: This lesson is not a prediction of conflict, and disruption scenario estimates from research groups vary widely and should never be treated as precise forecasts. The value of the exercise is structural: it forces you to map exactly which parts of a portfolio have direct exposure to Taiwan's leading-edge fabs, versus indirect exposure through global demand shocks, since the appropriate hedge for each is different.

body.title: Map the exposure
body.scenario: You manage a portfolio with three holdings: an Indian smartphone contract assembler that sources chips through global distributors, an Indian IT services company with major US and European technology clients, and an Indian company building mature-node chip packaging capacity under the PLI framework.
body.prompt: Rank these three holdings from most to least exposed to a severe, hypothetical disruption in Taiwan's advanced chip production, and briefly justify the ranking.
body.modelAnswer: The smartphone assembler is most exposed, since it directly needs advanced chips sourced through a global supply chain ultimately anchored in TSMC's leading-edge fabs, and any shortage would immediately halt or slow its production lines. The IT services company is exposed indirectly and with a lag: a severe global tech disruption would eventually hit its clients' capital spending and technology budgets, but this would take longer to materialise and would be more diffuse. The mature-node packaging company is least exposed in the near term, since it deals with less advanced chip technology that is more geographically diversified and less concentrated in Taiwan specifically, though it could see some indirect benefit if global demand shifted toward diversifying mature-node capacity as well.

body.title: Test the shield theory
body.question: According to the "shield is weakening" argument in this lesson, why does government-funded fab diversification create a paradox for Taiwan's strategic position?
options: It makes Taiwan's chips more expensive to produce
It reduces the rest of the world's dependence on Taiwan, which is precisely the dependence the shield theory relies on for deterrence
It has no effect on Taiwan's strategic position either way
It forces TSMC to lower its prices to compete with subsidized rivals
body.explanation: The paradox is that the same governments hoping to reduce their strategic vulnerability by diversifying chip supply are, by succeeding, gradually eroding the global economic interdependence that the Silicon Shield theory says protects Taiwan in the first place.

body.title: Semiconductors and the Taiwan Chokepoint: Core Terms

cards.definition: A chip company business model that designs chips but outsources all manufacturing, pioneered as viable at scale by companies like Apple, Nvidia and Qualcomm working with foundries like TSMC.
A company, like TSMC, that manufactures chips designed by other companies and designs none of its own, distinct from an Integrated Device Manufacturer.

The theory that Taiwan's dominance of advanced chip manufacturing deters conflict by making the global economic cost of disruption prohibitively high, a theory in tension with ongoing efforts to diversify chip production away from Taiwan.

Leading-edge nodes are the most advanced, smallest-transistor chip technologies, remaining concentrated in Taiwan; mature nodes are older, larger-transistor technologies increasingly being diversified to fabs in the US, Japan and Germany.

points: TSMC alone accounts for roughly 60% of the global pure-play foundry market, and well above 90% of production at the most advanced process nodes, making it a single-company chokepoint, not just a single-country one.
The fabless-plus-foundry model, pioneered by TSMC, is why companies like Apple and Nvidia design chips without owning a single fabrication plant.

The Silicon Shield theory holds that Taiwan's chip dominance deters conflict, but every dollar of CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act or India-style diversification funding very slightly weakens that same shield by design.
TSMC's overseas fabs in Arizona, Kumamoto and Dresden mostly handle mature nodes; the most advanced technology is staying concentrated in Taiwan for the foreseeable future.

India has little direct exposure to Taiwan's most advanced chip production today, since its own semiconductor push focuses on assembly, testing and mature-node fabrication, but it has substantial indirect exposure through global electronics and IT demand shocks.

Disruption-cost estimates from think tanks vary widely by methodology and should be treated as illustrative scenario modelling, useful for mapping portfolio exposure, not as precise forecasts of what will happen.
